Dozens of nations warn of famine in Sudan

Dozens of countries, including the United States and major European powers, have issued a joint statement warning of a worrying deterioration in food security in Sudan. Published by the US State Department, the statement cites the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), which has warned of a risk of famine in the coming months, and stresses that the parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for easing civilian suffering.

The signatories called on the warring sides to remove all obstacles to humanitarian aid, urged the international community to increase funding, and asked financial institutions to adapt existing programmes to the food crisis.

Sudan's army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, after disputes over integrating their forces during a planned transition to civilian rule. In June, the UN-backed IPC reported 5.1 million people facing severe hunger, as farmers struggle to harvest amid war and a recent wave of drought.

Source: Middle East Monitor

Israel Votes: No Majority, Arab Parties Pivotal

Early results from Israel's general election of 28 October 2026 show neither major bloc reaching the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority. With more than half of ballots counted, The Times of Israel projected Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc at 56 seats and Gadi Eisenkot's opposition alliance at 49. Likud is projected as the largest single party with 27–28 seats, ahead of Eisenkot's Yashar with 21.

According to the Central Elections Committee, Palestinian-led parties have overtaken Naftali Bennett's Together alliance for third place. At an earlier stage of counting, the Joint List and Ra'am were projected to win 16 seats combined, enough to give Eisenkot's bloc 63 seats if they chose to back it.

Speaking at Likud headquarters in West Jerusalem, Netanyahu said a right-wing government must be formed and ruled out relying on Arab parties, adding that the true results were one or two days away. Al Jazeera analyst Marwan Bishara noted that Likud's tally is its lowest since 2009. All figures remain provisional.

Source: Anadolu Agency, Al Jazeera, Middle East Eye

Türkiye Bets on Smaller, Sharper Defence Alliances

In a commentary for SETA dated 26 October 2026, Nebi Miş argues that large multi-member alliances struggle to take decisions on major issues, noting that the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the Arab League have for years failed to produce effective responses to their members' shared security crises. He points to the Mecca Medium Defence Agreement signed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan as potentially one of the most important security alliances of recent years.

An Anadolu Agency analysis examines a parallel track: on 21 October in Doha, Türkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia signed the Badr Memorandum of Understanding, aimed at strengthening defence-industry cooperation and laying the groundwork for technical military training. The piece highlights Qatar's investment-led approach and its ties with firms such as ASELSAN, STM and MKE, Pakistan's record in technical training and its links to programmes like KAAN, and Indonesia's joint drone and tank projects with Ankara. Türkiye signed 15 billion dollars in new defence contracts this year.

Source: SETA (Nebi Miş); Anadolu Agency Analysis

Iraqi PM in Damascus, eyes on oil

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi arrived in Damascus on 28 October 2026, the first visit by an Iraqi premier since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. Leading a high-level delegation, he was welcomed by Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa at Damascus International Airport.

According to the Iraqi prime minister's office, the talks covered exporting Iraqi oil through the Baniyas pipeline with a capacity of up to 2 million barrels per day, expanding trade and developing agriculture. In July, the two countries signed a memorandum to rehabilitate the Haditha–Baniyas pipeline, with Chevron expected to implement it. Iraq has begun exporting limited oil volumes via Syria since the US-led war on Iran, and is studying routes through Syria and Turkiye as alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz.

Zaidi described Iraqis and Syrians as "one people in two countries", while Sharaa stressed Syria's commitment to the highest levels of cooperation. Border security and counter-terrorism were also expected to feature.

Source: Al Jazeera, Middle East Monitor, TRT World

US Orders Diplomats Out of Saudi Arabia

The US Mission in Saudi Arabia said in a security alert dated 28 October 2026 that the State Department had ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave the kingdom, effective 23 October. It cited attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure, which caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions, and warned the hostilities could escalate rapidly.

US government staff now require special authorisation from the Chief of Mission to use any Saudi airport. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has partially reopened, with some flights shifted to Prince Naif bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Qassim, while Jeddah and Dammam report delays and cancellations.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki reported the interception of a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the Eastern Province, a day after another was downed near Taif. In Riyadh, debris from two intercepted missiles damaged a building, a construction project and a vehicle. Saudi Arabia has led a coalition against the Houthis since March 2015.

Source: Middle East Eye, Anadolu Agency

Libya’s Parliament Backs Türkiye Maritime Deal

On 20 October, Libya’s House of Representatives, meeting in Benghazi, unanimously approved the Memorandum of Understanding on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas signed with Türkiye in 2019. The chamber also lifted decision 2020/1, which had rejected the memorandum, and decision No. 6, which had called for severing political relations with Türkiye. The Government of National Unity in Tripoli viewed the decision positively.

Writing for SETA, Tunç Demirtaş describes the approval as an important strategic gain for Ankara’s Eastern Mediterranean policy, arguing that its significance cannot be separated from the security and connectivity order taking shape in the region. He notes that Türkiye advocates an inclusive cooperation mechanism, involving all littoral states, to support regional prosperity and stability.

Iran says four tankers ablaze in Hormuz

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says four tankers have caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz since early Friday, claiming the vessels struck naval mines while using what Tehran describes as 'unauthorised routes'. According to the IRGC navy's public relations office, the latest was a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil that ignored repeated radio warnings against using the southern passage before a mine triggered a powerful explosion.

Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that a vessel was struck on its port side by an unidentified projectile 40 nautical miles south of Iran's Lavan Island at 1800 GMT, causing a fire. The crew was reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded. It is not clear whether this incident is connected to the tanker reported by the IRGC.

The strait links the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is among the world's most important routes for oil and liquefied natural gas. Maritime tensions have persisted since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February. Despite a memorandum signed by Washington and Tehran in June, disputes over navigation and maritime security in the strait continue.

Source: Al Jazeera, Anadolu Agency
